analyst:
Virginia enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 27-4 team that finished 15-3 in ACC play, good for second in the league standings, and Virginia had already clinched the No. 2 seed in the ACC Tournament with a March 3 win over Wake Forest. Ryan Odom’s first Virginia team was 25-4 and 13-3 ACC entering that Wake game, then improved to 26-4 and 14-3 with the 75-70 win over Wake, and season results listed through March 10 show the Cavaliers at 27-4 overall and 15-3 in conference play. The basic profile is a major departure from late-era Tony Bennett tempo ball: through Dec. 10, Virginia was averaging 87.1 points per game, shooting .488 from the field and .400 from three, while even later-season reporting repeatedly described Odom’s identity as “play with pace, share the basketball,” and “dictate and disrupt” defensively. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/virginia/men/2026-schedule.html?utm_source=openai))

Offensively, Virginia is built around spacing, multiple ball-handlers, and frontcourt skill rather than a static mover-blocker structure. Thijs De Ridder is the centerpiece: Sports-Reference lists him at 15.9 points and 6.3 rebounds per game, and Virginia’s own recaps show the offense toggling between drive-and-kick threes and interior punishment through him. Against Boston College on January 31, when UVA shot only 4-for-23 from three, Odom’s team adjusted by pounding the ball inside; De Ridder went 7-for-10 from the floor for 17 points, and the official recap explicitly noted, “We tried it inside today, and it worked.” Against Wake Forest on March 3, when perimeter shots were being taken away early, assistant coach Matt Henry urged the team to attack the rim for easier looks; Jacari White responded by going 4-for-5 inside the arc and scoring 14 points, while Virginia hit 7-of-15 from three in the second half. The named tendencies are clear: early drag/transition attacks for White, spread pick-and-roll or slot action for Dallin Hall, and half-court touches for De Ridder that can become face-up drives, post seals, or kick-outs. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/virginia/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Hall is the control guard in close games, even though his scoring average is modest at 5.8 points in Virginia’s Dec. 10 combined stats and 5.8 in Sports-Reference’s season summary. His real value is organizational: he had 37 assists against 13 turnovers through 10 games, and Virginia trusted him to close against Wake Forest, where he made all four of his free throws in the final 15 seconds, including the last two with 5.2 seconds left. Chance Mallory, the freshman reserve guard, adds ball pressure and secondary creation; through 10 games he had 33 assists and 22 steals-adjacent disruptive plays were already visible, and later game notes listed him at 3.0 assist/turnover ratio and 2.0 steals per game entering the Ohio State game. Virginia’s offense is therefore not one-player heliocentric; it is a committee attack built on paint touches, quick reversals, and depth-based shot creation. ([storage.googleapis.com](https://storage.googleapis.com/virginiasports-com/2025/12/UVA_Combined_Stats.pdf))

Defensively, the philosophy is physicality, rim protection, and turnover creation without sacrificing rebounding. Odom’s own language before Boston College was that Virginia’s defensive style is to “dictate and disrupt.” The personnel fits that: Johann Grünloh and Ugonna Onyenso give Virginia two legitimate 7-foot rim protectors, and through 10 games UVA had 71 blocks in 10 games, 7.1 per game, while allowing opponents to shoot only .398 overall and .305 from three. Virginia’s February 7 win over Syracuse is a clean example of the system working. The Cavaliers had nine steals, scored 17 points off turnovers, outrebounded Syracuse 38-28, generated 17 second-chance points, and physically erased Syracuse star Donnie Freeman, who entered averaging 18.6 points per game but was held to five points on 2-of-11 shooting. In the February 3 win over Pitt, Virginia allowed only 47 points, and De Ridder grabbed 12 rebounds in a game that never became seriously threatened once UVA took control. ([virginiasports.com](https://virginiasports.com/news/2026/01/30/no-17-virginia-plays-at-boston-college-saturday-afternoon?utm_source=openai))

Odom’s adjustment history is already documented in specific games. The best example is January 27 at Notre Dame. Virginia trailed by 19 in the first half and was getting shredded by spacing; Notre Dame hit 8-of-13 threes and shot 57.7% in the first 20 minutes. Odom responded by abandoning the dual-7-footer look and playing smaller with De Ridder and Devin Tillis as the post players so Virginia could switch more, keep bodies in front, and pressure the ball. That tactical change fueled a comeback from 19 down to a 100-97 double-overtime win. Another example came March 3 against Wake Forest: with Wake running shooters off the line, Odom and assistant Matt Henry shifted emphasis from perimeter volume to rim attacks, and White’s transition pushes and interior drives became a deciding factor. Even in losses, Odom’s comments reveal process-driven coaching; after the Duke blowout referenced on March 3, Grünloh said Odom immediately refocused the team on “unfinished business in conference,” and Virginia answered by clinching the 2-seed against Wake. ([virginiasports.com](https://virginiasports.com/news/2026/01/27/no-17-hoos-storm-back-to-earn-double-overtime-win))

Clutch and late-game execution has been one of Virginia’s defining strengths, though not without some scars. The signature win is January 27 at Notre Dame: UVA won 100-97 in double overtime after trailing by 19, Sam Lewis hit a contested three with 3.5 seconds left in the first overtime to extend the game, and Virginia went 6-for-6 from the foul line in the final 71 seconds of the second overtime. On January 31 at Boston College, Odom praised the “execution down the stretch” after a road comeback win in which UVA finally separated late. On February 14 against Ohio State, Virginia’s composure showed again in a comeback win; a critical late sequence featured Devin Tillis grabbing the rebound of a missed Onyenso free throw and feeding Onyenso for a basket that put UVA ahead 61-59. On March 3 against Wake, Hall closed the game with four free throws in the last 15 seconds. The cautionary counterexample is December 31 at Virginia Tech: Virginia lost 95-85 in triple overtime in a game with 17 ties and 21 lead changes, and the official recap said that when the Cavaliers most needed a stop or defensive rebound, they could not deliver. ([virginiasports.com](https://virginiasports.com/news/2026/01/27/no-17-hoos-storm-back-to-earn-double-overtime-win))

Key players start with De Ridder, the most reliable matchup problem on the roster. Sports-Reference lists him at 15.9 points and 6.3 rebounds per game, and his late-January burst elevated Virginia’s ceiling: 32 points and eight rebounds at Notre Dame on January 27, then 17 points on 7-of-10 shooting at Boston College on January 31, then 16 points, seven rebounds, and three assists against Wake on March 3. Malik Thomas is the perimeter scorer; Sports-Reference lists him at 12.1 points per game, and he delivered 25 points against Louisville on January 13 while also making two key late threes versus Wake in the final eight minutes. Sam Lewis is the wing shot-maker and connective defender; he averages 10.4 points per game, scored 16 against Syracuse on February 7, and produced the biggest shot of Virginia’s season with the game-tying three at Notre Dame. Jacari White, at 8.9 points per game, is the microwave spacer whose role became more versatile after his return from a broken left wrist; he scored 14 against Wake and had eight points, three assists, and two steals versus Syracuse. Hall is the closer/organizer, and Onyenso plus Grünloh anchor the interior. Onyenso was cited at 2.6 blocks per game in late-February notes, and Grünloh’s late-season revival was evident in his 12 points, nine rebounds, and three blocks against Wake. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/virginia/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Notable wins show the range of this team. The December 3 road win at Texas, 88-69, proved Virginia could win away from home against brand-name competition, and De Ridder had 15 points in that one. The January 13 wire-to-wire win over Louisville showed Virginia could control an elite offensive opponent; Louisville came in averaging 88.3 points per game, but UVA handled transition, won the glass 44-36, and Malik Thomas scored 25. The January 27 win at Notre Dame revealed toughness and tactical flexibility. The February 7 win over Syracuse, 72-59, showed the defense can take over a game against a frontcourt-centric opponent. The March 3 win over Wake, 75-70, showed late-game poise and second-half shooting under pressure. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2025-12-03-21-texas.html?utm_source=openai))

The losses are instructive too. The November 23 neutral-court loss to Butler, 80-73, remains an early data point that physical half-court teams can drag Virginia out of rhythm. The December 31 triple-overtime loss at Virginia Tech exposed vulnerabilities on the defensive glass and in finishing possessions. The January 24 home loss to North Carolina, 82-70, revealed that turnovers can still swing games against high-end athletic opponents; Virginia had 11 turnovers to UNC’s four, and after building a 16-point first-half lead, UVA could not hold the margin. The late-February loss at Duke, referenced by Virginia’s March 3 recap as a one-sided defeat that ended a nine-game win streak, is the clearest warning sign against top-of-bracket talent. ([storage.googleapis.com](https://storage.googleapis.com/virginiasports-com/2025/12/UVA_Combined_Stats.pdf))

As for NCAA tournament history, the current head coach is Ryan Odom, not Tony Bennett. Odom’s documented postseason history before Virginia includes an NCAA Division II Sweet 16 at Lenoir-Rhyne in 2015-16, an NCAA Division I second round at UMBC in 2017-18 after the historic upset of Virginia, an NCAA first-round appearance at Utah State in 2022-23, and an NCAA first-round appearance at VCU in 2024-25. Virginia’s March 2 game notes list those finishes explicitly in his head-coaching record. That matters for scouting: this is a coach with a real adjustment background, upset-game credibility, and a roster specifically built to play faster, deeper, and more physically than the old Virginia stereotype. ([godeacs.com](https://godeacs.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/WF_030326.pdf))
forecaster:
Virginia enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with the profile of a legitimate top-four-seed caliber team, but the statistical shape of that résumé is more interesting than the brand-name shorthand suggests. On Warren Nolan’s 2026 team sheet, the Cavaliers are 29-5 overall, 15-3 in the ACC, and sit at NET No. 12. That same sheet lists Virginia’s predictive metrics at KenPom No. 13, ESPN BPI No. 20, and Bart Torvik T-Rank No. 14. The immediate takeaway is that the résumé and the predictive models are aligned on Virginia as clearly tournament-worthy and comfortably inside the national top 20, but not uniformly elite in the same way a top-five title favorite would be. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Virginia))

The strongest hard numbers I was able to locate for Virginia’s possession-level performance come from TeamRankings pages tied to the 2025-26 season. Those pages show Virginia with offensive efficiency around 1.19 points per possession and defensive efficiency around 0.97 points per possession, which translates to roughly 119.4 points scored and 96.9 points allowed per 100 possessions. TeamRankings also lists Virginia at 70.2 possessions per game, which is a major stylistic signal: this is not the ultra-slow, grind-you-down Virginia of the Tony Bennett peak years. This team plays at a solidly above-median tempo, and in practical terms that means its margin is built with volume as well as efficiency. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/terrapins-cavaliers-2025-12-20/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

The offensive Four Factors are especially impressive. TeamRankings lists Virginia with a 55.8% effective field-goal rate, a 13.1% turnover rate, a 39.8% offensive rebounding rate, and a 0.361 free-throw-attempts-per-field-goal rate. Its three-point attempt rate is 46.3%, meaning nearly half of its shots come from three. That is a modern shot profile paired with excellent ball security and overwhelming second-shot generation. Put differently: Virginia is not just making shots; it is creating a lot of extra possessions and avoiding empty trips. A 13.1% turnover rate is elite territory for a high-major offense, while a near-40% offensive rebound rate is the kind of figure usually associated with physically dominant frontcourts. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/terrapins-cavaliers-2025-12-20/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

Defensively, the numbers are strong even if they do not scream historically dominant. TeamRankings shows opponents posting just a 44.3% eFG% against Virginia, with only 29.8% opponent three-point shooting and 44.0% opponent two-point shooting. The Cavaliers’ block rate is listed at 10.4%, and they limit opponents to a 28.0% offensive rebound rate. The weak point, relatively speaking, is forced turnovers: opponents turn it over on only 13.5% of possessions. So Virginia’s defense is more about contesting, protecting the rim, cleaning the glass, and suppressing shot quality than about creating chaos. That matters in March, because it tends to travel well, but it also means they may be less equipped to manufacture easy offense if jump shooting goes cold. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/terrapins-cavaliers-2025-12-20/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

Schedule quality is the clearest reason the predictive models stop short of full-throated top-10 consensus. Warren Nolan lists Virginia’s NET strength of schedule at No. 66 and its non-conference NET SOS at No. 202. That is a respectable but not punishing overall slate, and the non-conference number in particular is soft for a team with protected-seed ambitions. The résumé quality is still very good: Virginia is 8-4 in Quadrant 1, 9-1 in Quadrant 2, and avoided bad losses entirely with 5-0 Q3 and 7-0 Q4 records. But a softer schedule can leave some uncertainty about just how portable the elite efficiency numbers are against the very top layer of the field. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Virginia))

Recent-form evidence points to a team that strengthened as the season matured. Virginia’s official opponent game notes for late February described the Cavaliers as 24-3 with an eight-game winning streak, and early March notes had them at 25-4 and nationally ranked No. 13 in the AP poll. Sports-Reference search results then show Virginia reaching 27-4 by March 7 after beating Virginia Tech 76-72. That sequence suggests a strong late-season rise after an earlier four-loss phase, consistent with the idea that Ryan Odom’s first Virginia team improved materially over the back half of league play. While I could not extract a clean public “last 10 games adjusted efficiency” table, the available record trail and ranking movement support the conclusion that Virginia was playing its best basketball entering March rather than fading into the bracket. ([gopack.com](https://gopack.com/documents/download/2026/2/23/NCST_022426.pdf?utm_source=openai))

The most important divergence from conventional wisdom is stylistic. “Virginia” still evokes crawl tempo, rock fights, and offense as an afterthought. The 2025-26 numbers say otherwise. This team is playing around 70 possessions per game, launching threes at a 46.3% rate, posting a 55.8% eFG%, and scoring about 1.19 points per trip. That is not classic Virginia basketball in the public imagination; it looks much closer to a modern spacing-and-glass offense that happens to retain Virginia’s traditional defensive shot suppression. In that sense, the eye test may undersell the offense because people are still seeing the uniform before seeing the data. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/terrapins-cavaliers-2025-12-20/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

There is also a subtler divergence in the other direction: because the team is ranked highly and owns a 29-5 / NET 12 résumé, casual observers may assume an overpowering, title-favorite defense. The numbers suggest “excellent” rather than “all-time.” A defensive efficiency around 96.9 per 100 possessions is very good, but the lack of forced turnovers means Virginia is not especially disruptive. If an opponent can survive the initial action, get shots up, and keep Virginia off the offensive glass on the other end, the Cavaliers are a bit more vulnerable than the brand implies. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/matchup/terrapins-cavaliers-2025-12-20/efficiency?utm_source=openai))

Overall, Virginia’s 2026 tournament profile is that of a balanced, analytically credible contender with one especially dangerous trait: the offense appears better than the national stereotype. The Cavaliers have top-15 caliber predictive standing by KenPom and Torvik, a top-12 NET, elite offensive process indicators, strong defensive shot suppression, and no real résumé blemishes. The caution flags are a middling schedule-strength profile and a defense that wins with structure more than havoc. But if you are building a forecast, the numbers describe a team that is efficient on both ends, modern in shot selection, excellent on the offensive glass, and trending upward late. That is a team capable of making the second weekend with real Sweet 16-to-Elite 8 upside, and one that could outperform the public’s outdated mental model of what “Virginia basketball” is supposed to look like. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Virginia))
matchup-analyst:
Virginia is not the old Tony Bennett slow-grind version; Ryan Odom’s 2025-26 team is a much more modern spread offense built on ball movement, second-shot volume, and frontcourt rim protection. Virginia enters the tournament 29-5 and 2nd in the ACC, averaging 80.6 points per game with a 67.9 adjusted tempo, an offensive efficiency of 1.22 points per possession, a defensive efficiency of 0.97, a 54.6% eFG on offense, and the nation’s No. 10 offensive-rebounding rate at 37.9%. Defensively, they allow a 45.3% eFG, rank fifth nationally in opponent eFG%, seventh in opponent 2-point percentage, and pair that with the nation’s second-highest block rate. Their core production comes from Thijs De Ridder (15.5 ppg, 6.2 rpg), Malik Thomas (12.4 ppg), Sam Lewis (10.8 ppg, 40.7% from three), Chance Mallory (9.5 ppg, 3.6 apg, 1.6 spg), Dallin Hall (4.3 apg), Johann Grünloh (7.2 ppg, 5.2 rpg, 2.2 bpg), and Ugonna Onyenso (6.7 ppg, 5.0 rpg, 3.0 bpg). The defining structural feature is size: De Ridder is 6-9, Lewis 6-7, Malik Thomas 6-5, Hall 6-4, Grünloh 7-0, Onyenso 7-0, and even reserve Devin Tillis gives them another 6-7/6-8-type forward body. ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/virginia-1677))

Style-of-play diagnosis: Virginia is best when the ball moves side-to-side before the paint touch or kick-out. Odom explicitly pointed to passing and quick decision-making as the identity of the offense after the Queens game, where UVA posted 1.541 points per possession, hit 15 threes, shot 53.3% overall, and recorded 14 assists after totaling only 14 assists combined in the previous two games. Queens threw 1-3-1, 2-3, and trap looks at them, and Virginia’s answer was to pass through the zone and create open threes rather than over-dribble. That tells you the exact disruptive tactic: make them play east-west laterally without easy reversal passes, and bait them into isolation dribbles. Odom himself said the team had been “seduced into the dribble and not the pass” after the Northwestern game. When opponents successfully break Virginia’s rhythm with mixed coverages and tempo disruption, the offense becomes less efficient and more perimeter-dependent. ([virginia.sportswar.com](https://virginia.sportswar.com/article/basketball/2025/11/28/virginia-quiets-queens-takeaways-from-uvas-bounce-back-win/))

Press and zone vulnerability: there is real evidence here, but it is situational rather than absolute. Pittsburgh used what was described as a “slow-the-game, lower-the-possessions zone press,” and Virginia shot only 44.1% overall and 35.5% from three. Syracuse copied the press intermittently and mixed man and zone in the half court; Virginia shot just 41.3% overall and 33.3% from three in that game. Over that three-game stretch, UVA played at 65, 59, and 63 possessions, below its 70.2-possession season norm cited in that report, and shot 43.8%, 44.1%, and 41.3% against teams in the bottom seven of the ACC standings. That is your cleanest evidence that changing tempo and coverages can drag them out of comfort. Counterpoint: early in the season, Queens tried multiple zones and traps and got shredded because Virginia passed decisively and kept turnovers down. So the actionable conclusion is not simply “play zone”; it is “play a changing zone/press menu that slows the game and interrupts first-side actions.” Static zone is not enough. ([virginia.sportswar.com](https://virginia.sportswar.com/article/basketball/2026/02/07/virginia-shakes-off-syracuse-takeaways-from-seasons-20th-win/))

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: Virginia’s pace is faster than past UVA teams but still not truly fast by national standards; 67.9 adjusted tempo ranks only 251st. Their best offensive version is controlled pace with flow, not chaos. They want enough tempo to get early offense and offensive-rebound pressure, but not a turnover game. To force the opposite, you want one of two extremes: either drag them into a 59-65 possession rock fight with zone press/mixed coverages, as Pittsburgh and Syracuse did, or force them into defensive scramble possessions with five-out spacing, as Notre Dame did early and Virginia Tech did over a full game. Notre Dame put Virginia in a 19-point first-half hole while shooting 57.7% in the first half and 8-of-13 from three before Odom downsized. Virginia Tech pushed UVA into a 95-85 three-overtime loss in which the key failure, per Virginia’s own recap, was inability to get stops and defensive rebounds late; 6-10, 260-pound freshman Christian Gurdak finished with 17 points and 19 rebounds. Those are the templates: either suffocate the possession count offensively, or stretch their shot-blockers and then punish the glass. ([virginia.sportswar.com](https://virginia.sportswar.com/article/basketball/2026/02/07/virginia-shakes-off-syracuse-takeaways-from-seasons-20th-win/))

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: at point guard, Hall is a pass-first organizer, but not an overwhelming downhill athlete; Chance Mallory is the better pressure guard, leading the team with 1.6 steals per game and 3.6 assists per game. A power guard who can collapse the lane without being blocked at the rim can pressure Hall physically. At the 2/3, Malik Thomas (6-5, 215) and Sam Lewis (6-7, 210) give Virginia length and switchability; smaller backcourts can get shot over. Lewis was decisive in the Notre Dame comeback with 21 points, 9 rebounds, and 6 assists, so opponents need a true wing stopper, not a small guard cross-matched onto him. At the 4, De Ridder is the major matchup issue: 15.5 ppg, 6.2 rpg, 50.8% FG, plus foul-drawing ability. Against Notre Dame he scored 32, drew nine fouls, and went 14-of-15 at the line. Against Virginia Tech he scored 22, but also committed six turnovers, which is important: strong, active hands can bother him when he puts it on the deck. At center, Grünloh and Onyenso give them elite shot blocking, but the evidence says mobile stretch lineups can force Odom smaller. Against Notre Dame’s spread floor, Odom said he had to use De Ridder and 6-7 Devin Tillis as post players so Virginia could switch more and keep bodies in front. That means a pick-and-pop five or five-out attack can pull the 7-footers into uncomfortable space and reduce Virginia’s rim deterrence. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/258/virginia-cavaliers))

Isolation vs. team offense tendencies: the clearest quantifiable signal is that Virginia is assist-driven, not iso-driven. They average 16.6 assists per game against only 10.8 turnovers, with Hall at 4.3 apg and Mallory at 3.6 apg. In the Queens reset game, seven players had at least two assists, which is classic team-offense behavior. When Odom complained about too much dribble and not enough pass after the Greenbrier stretch, that was effectively a coaching diagnosis that Virginia’s offense degrades when it leans into individual creation. I cannot verify a reliable public 2025-26 Synergy isolation-possession percentage from a primary source available on the open web, so I will not invent one. The best evidence-based inference is that this is a low-iso, high-decision, shared-possession offense because both coaching quotes and assist profile point that way. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/258/virginia-cavaliers))

Transition offense and defense: again, fully reliable public possession-frequency splits are limited on the open web, so the cleanest verified team-level numbers available are pace, offensive efficiency, turnover rate, and rebounding profile. Virginia’s offense is not built on reckless transition hunting; its 67.9 tempo and 13.5% turnover rate indicate controlled offense, while the 37.9% offensive-rebound rate shows they create extra possessions with the glass rather than sheer pace. The counterexample games matter most. Virginia Tech turned the game into repeated second-chance and scramble sequences, and UVA’s own recap specifically said the Cavaliers failed to get a stop or a defensive rebound when they needed one most. Notre Dame also made Virginia uncomfortable with floor spacing and perimeter shotmaking before Odom adjusted. So if you want transition opportunities against Virginia, the best route is not live-ball gambling first; it is stretch their rim protectors, force long rebounds, then run before the second line is set. ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/virginia-1677))

Coaching adaptability: yes, Odom has shown real in-game flexibility. The best example is Notre Dame on January 27, 2026. Virginia was down 19, gave up 57.7% first-half shooting and 8-of-13 from three, then changed personnel and coverage logic. Odom explicitly said Virginia used smaller lineups it “hadn’t played” so it could switch more, keep bodies in front, and apply better pressure. That is a concrete midgame tactical adjustment, not coach-speak. Virginia then won 100-97 in double overtime. The other side of adaptability is that when opponents keep them off balance with alternating presses and zone looks, as Pittsburgh and Syracuse did, the offense can stay muted for long stretches. So Odom adjusts, but you can still make him spend the game reacting instead of dictating. ([virginiasports.com](https://virginiasports.com/news/2026/01/27/no-17-hoos-storm-back-to-earn-double-overtime-win))

Concrete game plan: To beat Virginia, you must do five specific things. First, play changing coverages, not a static base: use a soft zone press to burn clock, then alternate between man, 2-3, and matchup looks; Pittsburgh and Syracuse showed that recipe can drag UVA into low-60s possession games and sub-45% shooting. Second, attack De Ridder physically on his dribble and on defensive rotations; he had 32 points at Notre Dame, but also four turnovers, and he had six turnovers at Virginia Tech. Third, space out the 7-footers with a stretch five or five-out lineups; Odom already showed he will bench the twin towers for smaller switching units when spread teams make them uncomfortable. Fourth, finish possessions with defensive rebounds; Virginia is 10th nationally in offensive-rebound rate, and they are dangerous because missed shots become extra threes or dump-offs. Fifth, have real wing size so Lewis and Thomas do not simply shoot over your guards. If you let Virginia pass freely, get second shots, and keep one rim protector parked in the paint, they can beat you in multiple ways. If you change coverages, flatten their pace, stretch the centers, and win the rebound battle, you can make them play the exact kind of uncomfortable game that already produced the Virginia Tech loss and the ugly offensive stretches against Pittsburgh and Syracuse. ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/virginia-1677))
